title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
pub: arXiv:2108.07258 (v3, 12 Jul 2022); Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI / Center for Research on Foundation Models report
author: Rishi Bommasani · Drew A. Hudson · Percy Liang · et al. (Center for Research on Foundation Models · Stanford HAI)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition by arguing that resource-intensive frontier development centralizes model and data ownership and creates persistent advantages for large firms, while recognizing community and open-source counterweights rather than claiming monopoly is inevitable.
qs: As a result, the ownership of data and models are often highly centralized, leading to market concentration (§5.6: ethics).

To counterbalance this centralization, there have been grassroots efforts to open source AI research such as Masakhane, EleutherAI, and HuggingFace, or build foundation models through distributed training.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, context-sensitive deployment by portraying foundation models as broadly capable but incomplete, emergent and poorly understood, with defects capable of propagating across downstream uses. It reinforces the cluster’s sociotechnical caution, though it does not directly establish legal task-level gains, verification practices or specific work-redesign models.
qs: Despite the impending widespread deployment of foundation models, we currently lack a clear understanding of how they work, when they fail, and what they are even capable of due to their emergent properties.
Homogenization provides powerful leverage but demands caution, as the defects of the foundation model are inherited by all the adapted models downstream.

kp.k: Foundation models represent an AI paradigm shift
kp.d: The report characterizes broadly trained, highly adaptable systems such as BERT, DALL-E and GPT-3 as a paradigm shift. It introduces “foundation models” to emphasize that these systems are central infrastructure for many downstream tasks but remain incomplete rather than finished, task-specific products.
qs: AI is undergoing a paradigm shift with the rise of models (e.g., BERT, DALL-E, GPT-3) trained on broad data (generally using self-supervision at scale) that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks.
We call these models foundation models to underscore their critically central yet incomplete character.

kp.k: Scale produces emergence and encourages homogenization
kp.d: The authors argue that scale generates new emergent capabilities and that effectiveness across many tasks encourages developers to reuse a smaller number of foundation models. This homogenization creates broad benefits but also propagates defects from an underlying model into every downstream system adapted from it.
qs: Though foundation models are based on standard deep learning and transfer learning, their scale results in new emergent capabilities, and their effectiveness across so many tasks incentivizes homogenization.
Homogenization provides powerful leverage but demands caution, as the defects of the foundation model are inherited by all the adapted models downstream.

kp.k: Capabilities and failures remain poorly understood
kp.d: Despite anticipated widespread deployment, the report says researchers lack a clear understanding of foundation models’ capabilities, internal operation and failure conditions, particularly because capabilities can emerge unexpectedly. The authors recommend interdisciplinary research reflecting the technology’s sociotechnical character.
qs: Despite the impending widespread deployment of foundation models, we currently lack a clear understanding of how they work, when they fail, and what they are even capable of due to their emergent properties.
To tackle these questions, we believe much of the critical research on foundation models will require deep interdisciplinary collaboration commensurate with their fundamentally sociotechnical nature.

kp.k: Law is one downstream application domain
kp.d: The report explicitly includes law alongside healthcare and education among the application domains affected by foundation models, while situating these applications within a wider analysis of technical capabilities, social impacts and legal and ethical considerations. The supplied document does not provide specific findings about legal tasks, lawyers, law-firm structures, pricing or professional regulation.
qs: This report provides a thorough account of the opportunities and risks of foundation models, ranging from their capabilities (e.g., language, vision, robotic manipulation, reasoning, human interaction) and technical principles (e.g., model architectures, training procedures, data, systems, security, evaluation, theory) to their applications (e.g., law, healthcare, education) and societal impact (e.g. inequity, misuse, economic and environmental impact, legal and ethical considerations).

Five parts: §1 Introduction (emergence and homogenization; social impact and the foundation models ecosystem; the future of foundation models; overview of the report); §2 Capabilities (language, vision, robotics, reasoning and search, interaction, philosophy of understanding); §3 Applications (healthcare and biomedicine, law, education); §4 Technology (modeling, training, adaptation, evaluation, systems, data, security and privacy, robustness, AI safety, theory, interpretability); §5 Society (inequity and fairness, misuse, environment, legality, economics, ethics of scale).

kp.k: Foundation models create concentrated security dependencies
kp.d: The authors describe foundation-model security and privacy as largely unexplored and characterize a widely reused model as a high-leverage single point of failure. They cite existing demonstrations of adversarial triggers and training-data memorization, while arguing that general-purpose applicability increases function-creep and dual-use risks.
qs: Security and privacy for foundation models is largely uncharted at present.

Fundamentally, foundation models are a high-leverage single point of failure, making them a prime target for attack: existing work demonstrates a variety of security vulnerabilities (e.g., adversarial triggers to generate undesirable outputs) or privacy risks (e.g., memorization of training data) for these models.
Further, the generality of foundation models compounds these concerns, intensifying the risk for function creep or dual use (i.e., use for unintended purposes).

kp.d: For security analysis, the report analogizes foundation models to operating systems. The comparison frames them as general infrastructure on which many applications depend, making weaknesses in the shared layer consequential across downstream uses.
qs: For security, we view foundation models as akin to operating systems in traditional software systems.

kp.k: Model ownership centralizes markets and decision-making power
kp.d: The report argues that frontier development has mainly occurred within large companies, concentrating ownership of models and data. It links this market concentration to centralized decision rights and power and, drawing on Brynjolfsson’s reported “Turing Trap” concept, warns that this could reduce income, mobility and opportunity for people without ownership.
qs: Another key determinant of foundation models' economic impact is who owns data and models.
In particular, pushing the frontier of foundation models has thus far primarily been the purview of large corporate entities.
As a result, the ownership of data and models are often highly centralized, leading to market concentration (§5.6: ethics).
In turn, this can lead to significant centralization of decision rights and power, reducing income and opportunities for those who don't have ownership.
This centralization of power can lead to an equilibrium where fewer people have social and economic mobility and opportunity, a situation that Brynjolfsson [2022] calls "The Turing Trap".

kp.k: Open initiatives may not close the resource gap
kp.d: The authors identify Masakhane, EleutherAI, Hugging Face and BigScience as community efforts intended to counterbalance concentration. They nevertheless predict that open models will remain substantially behind private models because training depends on massive quantities of data and computational resources.
qs: To counterbalance this centralization, there have been grassroots efforts to open source AI research such as Masakhane, EleutherAI, and HuggingFace, or build foundation models through distributed training.

However, it likely that the gap between the private models that industry can train and the ones that are open to the community will remain large due to foundation models' dependence on massive amount of data and computational resources (§5.3: environment).

Community efforts such as EleutherAI and Hugging Face's BigScience project are attempting to train large foundation models, but the gap between the private models that industry can train and the ones that are open to the community will likely remain large if not grow.

kp.k: Resource advantages raise barriers to model development
kp.d: The report distinguishes among academia, well-resourced AI startups and much larger technology companies. It argues that big technology firms possess exceptional infrastructure, user and data advantages, and predicts that rising development barriers will eventually make competition difficult even for comparatively agile startups.
qs: Further, today startups (OpenAI, Anthropic, AI21 Labs, etc.) are much more well-resourced than academia and can therefore still afford to train the largest foundation models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-3).
However, big tech companies are on a completely different level in terms of resources, especially in terms of the infrastructure, users, and data that come from their market position.

The fundamental centralizing nature of foundation models means that the barrier to entry for developing them will continue to rise, so that even startups, despite their agility, will find it difficult to compete, a trend that is reflected in the development of search engines [Radinsky 2015].

kp.k: Government infrastructure could narrow development inequalities
kp.d: As a policy response to unequal access to the resources needed for foundation-model development, the authors recommend government investment in public infrastructure. The document presents this as one possible way to close the resource gap rather than as an empirically established outcome.
qs: One way to close the resource gap is for the government to invest in public infrastructure.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bommasani et al. claim that foundation models enable broad downstream adaptation while concentrating technical risks and economic power.
pts.d: The supplied passages make cross-domain claims rather than specific predictions about legal services. The authors argue that scale produces emergent capabilities and that effectiveness across tasks encourages homogenization, allowing shared model defects to propagate downstream. They describe foundation models as a concentrated security and privacy vulnerability, with generality increasing the potential for unintended uses. Economically, they argue that centralized ownership of data and models leads to market concentration and can reduce income, opportunity and mobility for non-owners. They predict a persistent or growing resource gap between private and community models and rising entry barriers even for well-resourced startups. They identify public infrastructure investment as one possible response.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims with references to existing security research, observations about resource ownership, named community initiatives and a historical analogy; the supplied passages contain no quantitative tests of these claims.
pts.d: For security and privacy, the authors invoke existing demonstrations of adversarial triggers and training-data memorization, without providing study-level results in these excerpts. For concentration and entry barriers, they point to corporate dominance in frontier development, big technology companies' infrastructure, users and data, and the dependence of training on substantial computational and data resources. They name community efforts as countervailing initiatives and cite Radinsky (2015) for the search-engine analogy. Brynjolfsson (2022) supplies the 'Turing Trap' label for a possible outcome; the concentration argument is presented by Bommasani et al. The supplied record identifies the report as an arXiv preprint, not a peer-reviewed journal article, and provides no legal-market measurements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes contemporary observations from open-ended predictions, with no numerical forecast horizon.
pts.d: The source is a 2021 report with a July 2022 revision. Statements about current understanding, existing vulnerabilities and resource disparities concern that publication context. Widespread deployment is described as impending. The resource gap is predicted to remain large or grow, and entry barriers to continue rising, without specifying dates. The concentration consequences are framed as possibilities rather than inevitable outcomes. Dependence on large data and compute resources underpins the resource-gap prediction, while community efforts and government-funded infrastructure are presented as potential counterweights.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include downstream model developers and users, model and data owners, non-owners, academia, community projects and startups.
pts.d: Downstream applications inherit defects from their shared foundation model, while attacks and privacy failures create risks across the foundation-model ecosystem. Large corporate owners are positioned to concentrate market power and decision rights; people without ownership may lose income and opportunities. Academia and community projects face resource disadvantages relative to private developers. Startups are described as better resourced than academia but disadvantaged against big technology companies and increasingly exposed to entry barriers. Government is identified as a potential provider of public infrastructure. Although law appears in the report's application scope, these excerpts do not specify effects on lawyers, law firms, legal-service buyers or access to justice.
